bib.title: VIOLET : End-to-End Video-Language Transformers with Masked Visual-token Modeling

legacy_report:
SOURCE: VIOLET: End-to-End Video-Language Transformers with Masked Visual-token Modeling. Tsu-Jui Fu, Linjie Li, Zhe Gan, Kevin Lin, William Yang Wang, Lijuan Wang, Zicheng Liu (UC Santa Barbara, Microsoft). Preprint, arXiv 2111.12681v2, 16 Apr 2022 (v1 Nov 2021).

COVERAGE: I read all 71,512 of 71,512 chars: main text, Tables 1-8, Appendices A-E (downstream setup, masking strategy, VCR, qualitative examples, limitations) and the references. I skimmed the references for origins only. Figures 6-9 are qualitative images with no numbers.

HEADLINE FOR THE CALLER: **The paper has no frame-count ablation.** It never varies T. The only frame numbers are fixed design choices: T=4 in pretraining, T=5 for downstream tasks, and one cross-paper comparison (VIOLET with 5 frames beats ClipBERT with 16). The most useful frame claim it supports is that **5 sparsely sampled 224x224 frames with temporal modelling beat 16 mean-pooled frames by about 10 R@1 points**. Even this comparison confounds frame count with encoder and pretraining data.

Two architecture points matter for the note:
- **VIOLET does not pool before a language model.** It concatenates Video Swin features (one per frame) with word embeddings and feeds them into a single cross-modal BERT. The paper's argument is *against* pooling: mean pooling scores worst.
- **Retrieval needs one model pass per pair.** It is a binary match classifier on [CLS] for every text-video pair, not separate embeddings with dot-product search. So it is a reranker-style cross-encoder, not something you can index for multimodal RAG. The paper does not discuss retrieval cost.

LIMITS:
- **No frame-count sweep.** No sampling-strategy comparison (uniform vs other). No latency or inference-cost numbers. No seeds, variance or confidence intervals: every result is a single run.
- **The ClipBERT and MERLOT comparisons confound** frame count, encoder, resolution and data. MERLOT is greyed out as too expensive to compare directly.
- **Retrieval is a cross-encoder** (binary match per pair), so it is not an indexable embedding retriever.
- **The authors concede:** sparse frames only, and dense full-length video (for example TGIF-Count) is future work; no audio; trails CLIP-initialised CLIP4Clip; they "believe VIOLET can further improve with larger frame resolution and longer pre-training epoch if computational resources permit."
- **Dated:** a 2021 BERT-style fusion encoder with no LLM. It predates video-LLMs, so it does not speak directly to "pool before the language model".
- Hardware: finetuning on 8 V100s; pretraining 2,240 GPU hours.

BUILDS ON: ClipBERT (Lei et al., CVPR 2021) for sparse sampling; Video Swin Transformer (Liu et al., arXiv 2106.13230, 2021); BEiT (Bao, Dong, Wei, arXiv 2106.08254, 2021) for masked visual tokens; VIMPAC (Tan et al., 2021) for blockwise masking; DALL-E dVAE (Ramesh et al., 2021) and VQ-VAE (van den Oord et al., NeurIPS 2017); MERLOT (Zellers et al., NeurIPS 2021) for YT-Temporal and attended masking for MLM; Frozen in Time (Bain et al., ICCV 2021) for WebVid and joint image-video training; UNITER (Chen et al., ECCV 2020) for MRM; HERO (Li et al., EMNLP 2020) for MFM; BERT (Devlin et al., NAACL 2019).

CODE: none in the paper. The repository is cited as github.com/tsujuifu/pytorch_violet (footnote 1, p1). Equation 4 shows the fusion input, quoted verbatim: "h = CT([v + pv, [CLS], w + px])" (Sec 3.1, p3).

FIGURES:
- Fig 2 (p3), "Overview of the proposed end-to-end VIdeO-LanguagE Transformer (VIOLET), with Video Swin Transformer, Language Embedder, and Cross-modal Transformer..." It shows at a glance that frame features are not pooled: they are concatenated with text into a single fusion transformer.
- Fig 3 (p5), "Masking Strategy of MLM and MVM, including Blockwise Masking (BM) and Attended Masking (AM)." It makes the space-time block masking easy to see.
- Fig 4 (p7), "MVM accuracy vs. downstream performance..." It shows the scaling trend in one plot.
- Table 3 (p7) is the most useful exhibit for the note's mean-pool vs temporal-model point.
